that improper governmental activity constitutes the use of the organization's official authority or influence to commit a crime, fraud, or other serious and willful violation of law, or a willful misuse of public funds, willful breach of fiduciary duty, or willful or corrupt misconduct in office. The second condition is what places the attorney in the most precarious position of weighing the duty to protect the public interest against the risk of losing his or her license to practice law due to a violation of Section 6068(e). Without the protection provided by this bill, an attorney may in fact either remain silent, or resign from his or her job. This second condition is also what the Attorney General wishes to narrow to "felony conduct." Under the third scenario, an attorney may refer the matter directly to law enforcement or an oversight official if he or she reasonably believed that the actions of urging reconsideration and referring to a higher internal authority are futile and the seriousness of the circumstances required further action in order to prevent substantial harm to the public interest or to the organization. While it may be argued that this leaves the government lawyer a lot of leeway to decide that going through the internal mechanism of rectifying a potentially harmful situation is useless (because, perhaps, an internal report may only lead to a cover-up), the lawyer would still have to make a reasonable good faith effort to assess the seriousness of the situation and to determine whether the harm to the public interest or to the organization would be substantial if he or she does nothing more. Proponents argue that without the protections provided by this bill, the attorney may remain silent, resulting perhaps in harm to the public, or resign from the job (which is the alternative currently available under Rule 3-600), resulting in harm to the lawyer personally. d. Attorney action restricted to internal report for conduct constituting willful omission to perform official duty Under this bill, where the improper governmental activity simply involves the governmental organization's agent's willful omission to perform his or her official duty, an attorney would not be protected from discipline if he or she referred the matter directly to law enforcement or other appropriate authority with oversight responsibility. This would be in keeping with the Attorney General's position that a government attorney should advise and encourage a government agency or official to take the correct course of conduct first. e. No discipline against attorney for making referral to law enforcement Under this bill, an attorney who takes the second order of action, i.e., referral to the appropriate law enforcement or government official with oversight responsibility on the matter or governmental organization or official involved, is protected from disbarment, suspension, or other discipline, provided the attorney acted reasonably and in good faith in determining the propriety of making the referral. The language of the bill states that the referral "shall not be a cause for disbarment, suspension, or other discipline." It does not provide complete immunity in that the attorney may still have to defend himself or herself in a disciplinary proceeding brought for a violation of Section 6068(e). All it means is that if the attorney proves he or she acted reasonably and in good faith in making the determination, he or she may not be subject to discipline. e. No protection for further affirmative action initiated by attorney Under , the protections provided an attorney representing a governmental organization would end with the referral to the law enforcement agency or oversight official and subsequent disclosures required by that agency or official in the execution of their oversight responsibilities. Any further action initiated by an attorney outside of those described in the bill would be subject to disciplinary proceedings and sanctions for violations of Rule 3-600 or Section 6068(e). This is appropriate, as the exception to Section 6068(e) is supposed to be very limited and designed to give the government lawyer a narrow but clear pathway to bring improper governmental activity, under appropriate conditions to the attention of appropriate officials. 3. Attorney representing government has no affirmative duty to act even with knowledge of improper government activity An attorney representing any governmental organization who learns of improper governmental activity would have no affirmative duty to take any of the actions protected from disciplinary action by the State Bar. Thus, any whistleblowing decision is left to the individual attorney on what to do or how far up the ladder of authority to go, should he or she decide to address the situation. Although much of the information provided by the author and the COPRAC analysis of the proposed amendments to Rule 3-600 refer to government lawyers or attorney-employees of governmental organizations, the language of refers to an attorney who, "in the course of representing a governmental organization?learns of improper governmental activity." This definition could cover an attorney in private practice with a contract to perform general legal services to a city on an as-needed basis, for example, as well as an attorney in private practice who is hired as outside counsel by the city council in addition to their full-time city attorney to work on a specific case, as well as the city attorney himself or herself. In a footnote, the COPRAC report clarifies that the recommended rule should apply equally to any attorney in his or her representation of governmental clients, whether the attorney is an employee of the government or is a private attorney retained by a government agency. The committee believes that significant adverse consequences would flow from a rule that distinguishes between employees and other attorneys who represent governmental clients. "Imposing a less stringent duty on in-house government attorneys than on outside attorneys retained by the government would tend to imply that employee-lawyers provide a different type of service, or fulfill a different role, than outside counsel. In addition, a rule giving less protection to the confidentiality of information held by employee-attorneys could encourage governmental agencies to use outside counsel simply because outside counsel would owe a more stringent duty of confidentiality than an in-house governmental attorney." Thus would apply to any attorney representing a governmental organization, whether in-house or not. In the case of the attorney who is hired to provide services on an as-needed basis, or the attorney whose contract is tied to a specific case, the bill does not require that the confidential information learned by the attorney be tied to the matter for which he or she was retained or hired. Thus, any "improper governmental activity" learned by the attorney, though not related to the work he or she is supposed to perform for the governmental organization, may lead the attorney to refer the matter to a law enforcement agency or higher official with oversight responsibility on the organization. The State Bar's decision in the Ossias case needs clarification Proponents contend that the case of Department of Insurance attorney Cindy Ossias demonstrated the need to clarify an attorney's right to blow the whistle, when the client is a governmental organization or official. Ms. Ossias chose to come forward and expose wrongdoing by then-Commissioner Chuck Quackenbush, at the risk of losing her license to practice law. The State Bar investigated Ms. Ossias, and ultimately exonerated her, but its decision did not clarify when disclosure by an attorney would be protected or what public policies would justify disclosure. b. Federal case law supports recognition of public agency attorney's duty to the public In re Bruce Lindsay 158 F.3d 1263 (D.C. Cir. 1998) limits the government attorney-client privilege of the President and other government officials. The court held that when government attorneys learn, through communications with their clients, of information "related to criminal misconduct," or "pertinent to possible criminal violations," the clients may not, by asserting the government attorney-client privilege, prevent such information from being disclosed to a federal grand jury. (Id at 1278.) Reasoning that the Office of the President is simply a part of the federal government like any other "consisting of government employees doing government business," the court held that there is no basis in "legal authority nor policy nor experience" to even suggest that a federal entity can maintain the "ordinary common law attorney-client privilege" to preserve the confidentiality of information relating to a federal crime. "Reason and experience, duty, and tradition dictate" that the attorney must provide the information. (Id at 1272.) c. More than half of the states allow disclosure when attorney knows of client's intent to commit a crime As originally proposed, would have mirrored Hawaii's newly-adopted rule specifically addressing issues faced by public sector attorneys. That rule, according to the Hawaii State Bar Newsletter, "recognize[s] that public agencies and public officials are drawn from the ranks of human beings who, from time to time, commit criminal or other illegal acts. Such acts are, by nature, contrary to the public good. Hawaii's version [of the model rule] makes it clear that a government lawyer's obligation of confidentiality is to be measured against the public interest, and not that of an individual or agency." A survey by the Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (PEER) shows that while most states do not distinguish between public and private attorneys when it comes to the duty of confidentiality, more than half of the states allow all attorneys to disclose a client's intent to commit a crime even if the disclosure includes revealing confidential communications. Under all of these rules (adopted by more than half the states), public sector attorneys can disclose information related to government entity wrongdoing without risking sanction by the particular state bar. In fact, California is the only state that prohibits disclosure of confidential information even when an attorney knows of the client's intent to commit a crime likely to result in death or bodily injury. Additionally, the American Bar Association has proposed amendments to Model Rule 1.6 related to confidentiality which track other states' efforts to recognize the unique duties of public agency attorneys. d. There are 14 currently known "families" or classes of synthetic cannabinoids. The bill appears to include them all. The EMCDD noted that 105 individual chemicals in these classes were being monitored in Europe in 2014. This bill includes hundreds of individual chemicals in the list of prohibited synthetic cannabinoids. Many of the chemicals are identified through a letter and number combination, such as JWH-018, AM-087 and HU- 210. The letters are generally the initials of the researcher who first synthesized the chemical or the institution where the research was done. The background provided by the author and sponsor includes model statutes for prohibiting synthetic cannabinoids and synthetic stimulants. The model statute was drafted by the National Alliance for Model State Drug Laws. (http://www.namsdl.org/about.cfm.) The list of chemicals in the bill reflects the model statute. The purpose of describing synthetic cannabinoids by class or family is to include any new chemical in each class as a prohibited substance. That is, if a new drug is developed in any of the 14 classes, the chemical is prohibited, regardless of whether the individual chemical is included in the statute. It is not known whether many new synthetic cannabinoid classes can or will be developed. Synthesis of a new class or family of cannabinoids would not be included in the list of prohibited chemicals. From 2010 through 2011, reported emergency room (ER) visits linked to synthetic cannabinoids increased from 11,406 to 28,531. The vast majority of patients were young males, ages 12 through 20.
